# CLOSE ROUND: DEFENDER

I hold D1 to D6 as declared. The challenger's blocks C1 to C6 are answered below under the link each one presses.

Two points govern the whole round.

- Matthew 1:18 puts the source of the pregnancy at the finding: "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost." [L2] *synerchomai* (G4905), "come together," includes conjugal cohabiting. The finding precedes the cohabiting, and the source is named in the same clause.
- Matthew 1:20 gives the reason for the command: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." [L2] *phobeō* (G5399) is "be afraid." [L4] The source "of the Holy Ghost" is what answers Joseph's fear. This rests on Matthew 1:19 ("minded to put her away privily") and Matthew 1:20 ("fear not ... for"). If the child were Joseph's, that answer would answer nothing.

---

## D1: begetting assigned to the Holy Ghost

ANSWER: 1 John 5:1 -- D1 -- "every one that loveth him that begat loveth him also that is begotten of him."
- [L2] *gennaō* (G1080) carries "to regenerate" as a figurative sense. [L3] 1 John 4:7 says "every one that loveth is born of God."
- The object in 1 John is a believer who already exists and has a human father. The verse itself conditions it on belief.
- Matthew 1:20's object is "that which is conceived in her," the child in the womb. Its source is stated in Matthew 1:18 at the finding, "before they came together."
- [L4] The 1 John usage is figurative because its object already has a human origin. Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 name the source of the conception itself, so the figure does not carry over.

ANSWER: 2 Samuel 12:24 -- D1 -- "went in unto her, and lay with her: and she bare a son."
- Solomon's row states the act of union. The rows for Mary state the opposite act: Matthew 1:25, "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
- 1 Chronicles 28:6 ("I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father") sits beside a stated union. Matthew 1:18 and 1:25 sit beside a stated absence of union.
- [L4] The same shape cannot be assumed for Joseph. The rows that surround Mary and Joseph differ from the rows surrounding David and Bathsheba.

---

## D2: Matthew 1:16 names Joseph husband, not begetter

ANSWER: Matthew 1:16 -- D2 -- "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."
- [L2] The relative "whom" is feminine, and *gennaō* is passive, "was born."
- [L3] Matthew 1:6: "David the king begat Solomon of her [that had been the wife] of Urias." Matthew names the mother there and still keeps "begat" for the father.
- At 1:16 he keeps "begat" for Jacob and Joseph and withholds it from Joseph and Jesus.
- [L4] The pattern runs on 1:2 to 1:15 ("Abraham begat Isaac"). It stops where the verb turns passive and feminine.
- Matthew 1:6 shows that naming the mother does not cancel the father's "begat." The break at 1:16 is therefore a break in the verb, not in the mother's mention.

ANSWER: Genesis 4:25 -- D2 -- "And Adam knew his wife again; and she bare a son."
- The row states "Adam knew his wife" before "she bare." Matthew 1:16 has no "knew."
- The nearest row, Matthew 1:25, says "knew her not till she had brought forth."
- [L4] The comparison fails on the verb that matters.

ANSWER: Exodus 6:23 -- D2 -- "she bare him Nadab, and Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar."
- "She bare him" is the phrase for a father's sons. The angel to Mary says no such thing.
- Luke 1:31: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son." The words "bear thee" are absent.

---

## D3: Luke 1:34-35

ANSWER: Luke 1:34 -- D3 -- "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
- [L2] *ginōskō* (G1097) "know" and *anēr* (G435) "a man." [L3] Genesis 4:1 uses "knew Eve his wife" for the marital act.
- Mary asks how, and the answer does not say "when Joseph takes you."
- Luke 1:27 names him: "a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph." The angel's answer in Luke 1:35 does not use his name.
- [L4] Mary asks about the means. The means given is the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, not Joseph.

ANSWER: Luke 1:35 -- D3 -- "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
- [L2] *epercomai* (G1904) "come upon" and *episkiazō* (G1982) "overshadow." "Therefore" (*dio*) is a consequence word inside the same verse, so it follows the clause just before it.
- [L3] Acts 1:8: "ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you."
- [L3] Luke 9:34: "there came a cloud, and overshadowed them."
- The challenger says these verbs mean "power and presence." Granted. The answer to "How" is God's power and presence in place of a man.
- Luke 1:32 gives the title before the question. Verse 35 states why this holy thing, the one born of Mary, is called by it.
- [L4] Luke 1:34 asks how a conception can come with no man, and Luke 1:35 answers by divine power.

ANSWER: Luke 1:13 -- D3 -- "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son."
- The angel tells Zacharias "bear thee." [L3] Luke 1:31 tells Mary only "thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son."
- [L4] Luke 1:13 and 1:31 differ in the angel's own words, so the husband-phrase is absent in the Mary row.

ANSWER: Luke 1:36 and Luke 1:37 -- D3 -- "she hath also conceived a son in her old age" and "For with God nothing shall be impossible."
- Luke 1:36 names the sign that follows Mary's question. Verse 37 gives the ground, "with God."
- [L4] The "also" joins the two as works of God's power. Elisabeth's husband is named in 1:13. The answer to Mary names the Holy Ghost, not a husband.

ANSWER: Luke 1:31 and Matthew 1:21 -- D3 -- "shalt call his name JESUS" and "thou shalt call his name JESUS."
- [L3] The naming is given to Mary in Luke 1:31 and to Joseph in Matthew 1:21.
- [L4] Naming is given to both, so naming is not a mark of begetting. The same table of rows gives Mary the name and Joseph the name.

---

## D4: virgin, and "knew her not"

ANSWER: Matthew 1:25 -- D4 -- "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
- The challenger bounds the not-knowing to after the taking. Matthew 1:18 puts the finding "before they came together."
- Matthew 1:24 puts the taking after the dream: "took unto him his wife."
- [L4] The challenger needs a knowing before 1:18's "found with child." Matthew 1:18 names the source of the pregnancy at the finding as "of the Holy Ghost," so no union stands before it. Verse 25 then covers the time through to the birth.

ANSWER: Genesis 4:1 -- D4 -- "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived, and bare Cain."
- It states Adam's act. It states nothing of Joseph. The row about Joseph is Matthew 1:25: "knew her not."

ANSWER: Deuteronomy 22:23 -- D4 -- "If a damsel [that is] a virgin be betrothed unto an husband."
- The law itself calls the betrothed damsel "a virgin." Betrothal is not union.

ANSWER: Deuteronomy 20:7 -- D4 -- "hath betrothed a wife, and hath not taken her."
- The same law uses "wife" of one not yet taken. So "thy wife" in Matthew 1:20 and "husband" in Matthew 1:19 are betrothal titles and do not imply a union.
- [L3] Luke 2:5 confirms it: "Mary his espoused wife, being great with child." She is "espoused" even while great with child.

ANSWER: Matthew 1:19 -- D4 -- "Then Joseph her husband, being a just [man], and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."
- [L2] *boulomai* (G1014) "minded." [L3] Matthew 1:20 answers: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife."
- [L4] An intent to put her away answers the pregnancy, which was found "before they came together" (Matthew 1:18). It fits a husband who knew the child was not his.

---

## D5: "supposed" and "father" as legal and household usage

ANSWER: Luke 3:23 -- D5 -- "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."
- [L2] *nomizō* (G3543) "suppose, be wont." The challenger glosses it as law and usage. That concedes D5, which says legal and household usage.
- [L3] Luke 4:22: "Is not this Joseph's son?" [L3] John 6:42: "whose father and mother we know?" Both are the townspeople's words, not the narrator's.

ANSWER: John 6:42 -- D5 -- "whose father and mother we know? how is it then that he saith, I came down from heaven?"
- The speakers are the people. [L3] Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law."
- [L4] The verse puts the people's supposition against his own claim of origin.

ANSWER: Luke 2:48 and Luke 2:49 -- D5 -- "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing" and "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"
- Mary's "thy father" is answered at once by "my Father's business." The reply sets a second Father against the first.
- [L2] *patēr* (G3962) is "near or more remote."
- [L3] 1 Chronicles 28:6: David's son Solomon is chosen "to be my son," with "I will be his father." [L3] 2 Samuel 7:14: "I will be his father, and he shall be my son."
- Those rows sit beside a stated union (2 Samuel 12:24). Luke 2:48 and 2:49 are two fathers named in successive verses, and Luke 2:49 corrects the first.
- [L4] Luke 2:49 corrects Mary's usage.

ANSWER: Luke 2:33, Luke 2:41, Luke 2:27 -- D5 -- "And Joseph and his mother marvelled," "his parents went to Jerusalem every year," "when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him after the custom of the law."
- At Luke 2:33 the narrator writes "Joseph," not "father." [L2] *goneus* (G1118) is "parent."
- [L4] The household and its legal custom are in view. These rows do not state begetting.

ANSWER: Deuteronomy 25:6 -- D5 -- "the firstborn which she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother [which is] dead, that his name be not put out of Israel."
- Law assigns a name to a man who did not beget the child. [L3] Genesis 48:5: "thy two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, ... [are] mine."
- [L3] Esther 2:7: "whom Mordecai, when her father and mother were dead, took for his own daughter."
- [L4] In Deuteronomy 25:6, Genesis 48:5 and Esther 2:7, the name or standing of father and child belongs to a man who did not beget. So Numbers 1:2 ("by the house of their fathers") and Ezra 2:61-62 show register by law and house.

ANSWER: Luke 2:4 -- D5 -- "because he was of the house and lineage of David."
- The row gives Joseph's house. [L4] It supports Joseph's legal line under Numbers 1:2 and does not state who begat the child.

ANSWER: Luke 3:31 -- D5 -- "which was [the son] of Nathan, which was [the son] of David."
- [L2] *huios* (G5207) "son," used of "immediate, remote or figuratively, kinship." Luke's list opens at "the son of Joseph" after "supposed." Both lists run by Joseph's legal line.

---

## D6: no human biological father

ANSWER: Romans 1:3 -- D6 -- "made of the seed of David according to the flesh."
- [L2] The verb *ginomai* (G1096) is "to come into being," not *gennaō*. [L2] *sarx* (G4561) is "the means of kindred."
- [L3] Genesis 3:15: "between thy seed and her seed." The woman has a seed.
- [L3] Galatians 4:4: "made of a woman."
- The flesh is of David and of the woman. [L4] Romans 1:3 requires descent from David and does not require Joseph's seed.

ANSWER: Acts 2:30 -- D6 -- "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh."
- The loins named are David's. [L3] Hebrews 7:10: "he was yet in the loins of his father, when Melchisedec met him." That father was an ancestor, so "loins" covers descent across generations.
- [L3] Hebrews 7:14: "our Lord sprang out of Juda."

ANSWER: 2 Samuel 7:12 -- D6 -- "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels."
- The row is about Solomon's line and promises a seed in David's descent. It does not say the seed of Jesus came through Joseph's loins.
- [L3] Luke 1:32, spoken to Mary: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David."

ANSWER: Jeremiah 22:30, Haggai 2:23, Matthew 1:12, Luke 3:27 -- D6 -- "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David."
- D1 to D6 do not rest on the Coniah sentence, and I rest nothing on it. The challenger's Haggai reply is an answer to a limb I did not declare. I leave it unadded.

---

## Conclusion

Matthew 1:18 names the source of the pregnancy at the finding, "before they came together." Matthew 1:20 repeats it as the reason Joseph should take his wife. Matthew 1:25 says "knew her not till she had brought forth." Luke 1:34-35 asks "How" and answers with the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest. Luke 3:23 marks Joseph's sonship as "supposed," and Luke 2:49 answers Mary's "thy father." The challenger's answers rest on rows about Adam, David and Aaron that state a union, and on betrothal titles that the law itself gives without union. I keep D1 to D6.

# Challenger's Answer: Christ Had a Biological Father, Joseph, of the House of David

**My reading.** The promised seed is David's *according to the flesh*, out of David's loins and bowels. The text carries that seed down the fathers' line to Joseph, "thou son of David." "Of the Holy Ghost" marks where the child comes from by covenant. It is said in the very row that names Joseph and "Mary thy wife," and it does not name a begetter. I press each link D1 to D6 below, aiming at the keystone D6.

---

## My chain (C1 to C4)

**C1. The promise requires seed out of a man's body.**
[L1] 2 Samuel 7:12: "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels, and I will establish his kingdom."
[L2] "Seed" is *zera'* (H2233), seed, posterity. At Romans 1:3 the Greek is *spermatos* (G4690), seed, and the phrase is *kata sarka*, according to the flesh.
[L3] Romans 1:3: "which was made of the seed of David according to the flesh." Acts 2:30: "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne." Hebrews 7:10 shows what "loins" means: "For he was yet in the loins of his father." There *osphys* (G3751) means loins, the procreative power, and it is set beside *patēr* (G3962), father.
[L4] 2 Samuel 7:12 says the seed comes "out of thy bowels." Acts 2:30 says it comes out of "his loins, according to the flesh." Hebrews 7:10 places the seed "in the loins of his father." So the seed the promise names passes through fathers' loins. It reaches the Christ "according to the flesh," not by naming alone.

**C2. The tribe is reckoned by the father's house.**
[L1] Hebrews 7:14: "For it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda; of which tribe Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood."
[L3] Numbers 1:18: "they declared their pedigrees after their families, by the house of their fathers." Numbers 1:2: "by the house of their fathers... every male by their polls." The reverse case is Ezra 2:61-62. Priests who took a wife of Barzillai's daughters and "was called after their name... were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood."
[L2] "House of their fathers" is *bayith* (H1004), house or family, with *'ab* (H1), father.
[L4] Hebrews 7:14 calls Judah's line "evident." Numbers 1:18 declares pedigree "by the house of their fathers." Ezra 2:62 strikes a register reckoned by the wife's name. So what made the tribe "evident" is a father's house. The one house the text names for this child is Joseph's: "he was of the house and lineage of David" (Luke 2:4).

**C3. The father is named, in four voices.**
[L1] Mary speaks: "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing" (Luke 2:48). The narrator speaks: "his parents went to Jerusalem every year" (Luke 2:41) and "Joseph and his mother marvelled" (Luke 2:33). A disciple speaks: "Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph" (John 1:45). The angel speaks: "Joseph, thou son of David" (Matthew 1:20).
[L2] "Parents" is *goneis* (G1118), parents, begetters. It is the narrator's own word at Luke 2:41 and Luke 2:27, "when the parents brought in the child Jesus."
[L4] Luke 2:41 and 2:27 are the narrator's voice, not the crowd's supposition. *Goneis* names the two as the child's begetters. Luke 2:48 puts "thy father" in the mouth of the woman who heard the angel. So the father the text names is Joseph.

**C4. The union stands inside the marriage the text names.**
[L1] Genesis 4:1: "And Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived."
[L3] Matthew 1:19: "Joseph her husband." Matthew 1:20: "Mary thy wife." Deuteronomy 22:24 calls a betrothed damsel "his neighbour's wife." Matthew 1:25: "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
[L2] "Till" is *heōs* (G2193), until. It bounds a span.
[L4] Genesis 4:1 gives knowing as the means by which a wife conceives. Matthew 1:19-20 and Deuteronomy 22:24 make Joseph and Mary husband and wife from the espousal. Matthew 1:25 bounds the abstinence to the span "till she had brought forth," which follows the taking of Matthew 1:24. So Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal, and the child is of his loins (C1).

## Presses against the declared chain

### LINK D1: Matthew 1:18 and 1:20

[L1] Matthew 1:20, whole: "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." Its margin reads "conceived: Gr. begotten."
[L2] The verb is *gennaō* (G1080), beget, here passive: "that which is begotten." The passive names no begetter. The source word is *ek* (G1537), out of. The phrase *kata sarka*, according to the flesh, which Romans 1:3 adds when flesh-descent is meant, is absent from this row.
[L3] 1 John 5:1 joins the same verb to God, said of believers: "Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God... every one that loveth him that begat loveth him also that is begotten of him." 1 John 4:7 says the same: "every one that loveth is born of God." Those believers were each begotten of a father in the flesh.
[L4] The defender reads "of the Holy Ghost" with *gennaō* as a begetting of the flesh. In 1 John 5:1 the same verb with "of God" names a covenant origin in men who have fathers. Matthew 1:20 leaves out the *kata sarka* that Romans 1:3 carries. So D1's step, "Matthew assigns the begetting to the Holy Ghost," reads a covenant-origin phrase as paternity. The row's own named man is "Joseph, thou son of David."

[L1] The defender says "Joseph's worry would make no sense if he were the father." Matthew 1:19 states Joseph's grounds: "being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."
[L2] *Eboulēthē*, "was minded," is a verb of intent, not a verb of knowing.
[L4] Matthew 1:19 gives the grounds as justness and an unwillingness to shame her. *Eboulēthē* reports what he intended, not what he knew. So the inference about his worry rests on a ground the verse does not give.

### LINK D2: Matthew 1:16

[L1] Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus."
[L3] Matthew 11:11: "Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist." John's father is named at Luke 1:13: "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son."
[L2] *Egennēthē*, "was born," is passive. The feminine *hēs*, "of whom," names the mother as the one who bore. "Born of women" at Matthew 11:11 is the same passive verb.
[L4] Matthew 11:11 says "born of women" of John, whose father Luke 1:13 names. So the passive with a mother named does not unname a father. Matthew 1:16 also carries the line "Jacob begat Joseph" to Joseph himself. Romans 1:3 requires "the seed of David according to the flesh" to reach the child, and the genealogy brings it to Joseph. So D2's word "exclude" goes past what its own verse states.

### LINK D3: Luke 1:34-35

[L1] Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee."
[L2] "Come upon" is *eperchomai* (G1904), come upon. "Overshadow" is *episkiazō* (G1982), overshadow.
[L3] Acts 1:8 uses the same verb with the same subject: "ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses." Its margin reads "or, the power of the Holy Ghost coming upon you." Luke 9:34 uses the second verb: "there came a cloud, and overshadowed them." Acts 5:15 does too: "that at the least the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow some of them."
[L4] In Acts 1:8, *eperchomai* with "the Holy Ghost" gives power to apostles. In Luke 9:34 and Acts 5:15, *episkiazō* is a cloud's presence and a healing shadow. So the angel's two verbs, read at their own rows, name empowering and presence. D3's "conception is by divine action and not by a man" adds a begetting the verbs do not carry.

[L1] Luke 1:32: "and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David."
[L2] "Therefore also" in Luke 1:35 is *dio kai*, on which account also.
[L4] The *dio kai* of verse 35 connects back to verse 32, not forward to a divine paternity of flesh. The title and "the throne of his father David" are given in Luke 1:32, before Mary asks "How shall this be" in Luke 1:34.

[L1] Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
[L2] *Ou ginōskō*, "I know not," is present indicative. It states her condition at the moment she spoke.
[L3] Luke 1:27 calls her "a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David."
[L4] Luke 1:34 states her present state. Luke 1:27 sets that state inside her espousal to Joseph. So D3's word "replaces" carries her present state forward into a permanent one the tense does not give.

### LINK D4: Isaiah 7:14, Matthew 1:23, Matthew 1:25

[L1] Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." Its margin reads "or, thou, O virgin, shalt call."
[L2] "Virgin" here is *almah* (H5959), 7 verses in the served record. The KJV prints that word as "maid" at Exodus 2:8 ("the maid went and called the child's mother") and "damsels" at Psalm 68:25. The defender's L3, Genesis 24:16, reads "a virgin, neither had any man known her." There "a virgin" is *bethulah* (H1330), a different Hebrew word.
[L4] The phrase "neither had any man known her" stands at Genesis 24:16 beside *bethulah*. The defender's almah rows, Genesis 24:43, Exodus 2:8 and Psalm 68:25, carry no such phrase. So the D4 footing borrows one word's clause to explain the other.

[L1] Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."
[L3] Matthew 1:24: "and took unto him his wife." Matthew 1:18: "before they came together, she was found with child."
[L4] Matthew's order is the finding (1:18), then the taking (1:24), then "knew her not till" (1:25). Verse 25 covers the span after the taking. Matthew 1:18 dates the finding before the coming together that 1:24 narrates. So D4's "No marital union therefore stands between the espousal of Matthew 1:18 and the child's conception" stretches 1:25 back over a span before the taking, which its "till" does not cover. Throughout that span she is "Mary thy wife" (1:20). I state the union at C4.

### LINK D5: Luke 3:23 and 2:49

[L1] Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."
[L2] *Enomizeto* is from *nomizō* (G3543), to do by custom, to suppose. It is the same form as Acts 16:13, "where prayer was wont to be made."
[L3] Luke 2:41: "his parents went to Jerusalem every year." Luke 2:48: "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing."
[L4] At Acts 16:13, *enomizeto* names a customary fact, not a false opinion. Luke's own narration calls the two "his parents" (2:41). So "as was supposed" carries no verdict against Joseph by itself. It stands with Mary's "thy father."

[L1] Luke 2:49 answers with "my Father's business." 2 Samuel 7:14 says of David's son: "I will be his father, and he shall be my son."
[L3] 1 Chronicles 28:6: "Solomon thy son... for I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father."
[L4] 1 Chronicles 28:6 names David's begotten son and God's covenant son in one verse, and neither name removes the other. So Luke 2:49 sets the covenant Father beside "thy father" of 2:48 without correcting Mary. D5's "Jesus corrects the use of 'father'" has the child correcting his mother's words where the pattern of 1 Chronicles 28:6 holds both fathers together.

### LINK D6, the keystone: Galatians 4:4, Genesis 3:15, Hebrews 10:5

[L1] Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law."
[L3] Job 14:1: "Man that is born of a woman is of few days." Genesis 4:25: "Adam knew his wife again; and she bare a son... For God, said she, hath appointed me another seed."
[L2] "Woman" is *gynē* (G1135), woman, wife. "Seed" at Genesis 4:25 is *zera'* (H2233).
[L4] Job 14:1 uses "born of a woman" for mortal man. At Genesis 4:25, Eve calls Seth her "seed" after "Adam knew his wife." So "made of a woman" and "her seed" name the mother and leave the father standing. Hebrews 2:14 says "he also himself likewise took part of the same," and Hebrews 2:17 says "in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren." His flesh came as his brethren's came.

# Closing the Challenge: The Seed of David According to the Flesh, Through Joseph, Thou Son of David

The defender's keystone (D6) needs two things. It needs Davidic flesh routed through a line the text does not name, and it needs "of the Holy Ghost" read as a begetter. Below I answer the defender's round 2 point by point, showing in each case how the witness fits my chain. The list follows.

## A. The question: how is it evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda?

[L1] Ezra 2:61: "which took a wife of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite, and was called after their name."
[L3] Ezra 2:62: "These sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but they were not found." Numbers 1:18: "they declared their pedigrees after their families, by the house of their fathers."
[L2] "House of their fathers" is *bayith* (H1004), house or family, with *'ab* (H1), father.
[L4] Ezra 2:61 says the name these men were "called after" was the wife's house, Barzillai's daughters. Ezra 2:62 says the genealogy register was searched for them and they were "not found." Numbers 1:18 keys that register to "the house of their fathers." So the register fails where the name comes from the wife's house. Ezra 2:61-62 confirms that reckoning runs by the father's house. The house that makes Judah "evident" (Hebrews 7:14) is the one Luke 2:4 names: Joseph "was of the house and lineage of David."

**The defender's adoption rows.**
[L1] Esther 2:7: "his uncle's daughter... whom Mordecai, when her father and mother were dead, took for his own daughter." Genesis 48:5: "thy two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, which were born unto thee in the land of Egypt."
[L2] At Romans 1:3 the word is *sperma* (G4690), "something sown, i.e. seed (including the male 'sperm')," and it comes with *kata sarka*, according to the flesh.
[L4] Esther 2:7 calls Esther Mordecai's kin, "his uncle's daughter," and Genesis 48:5 calls Ephraim and Manasseh Joseph's sons, "born unto thee." Romans 1:3 asks for seed, *sperma*, "according to the flesh." A taking-for-a-daughter supplies a household; Romans 1:3 names sown seed. So the adoption rows fit a household. The promise of Romans 1:3 stands on seed.

**The defender's "woman's seed" rows.**
[L1] Genesis 16:10: "I will multiply thy seed exceedingly."
[L3] Genesis 16:15: "Hagar bare Abram a son." Genesis 4:25: "Adam knew his wife again; and she bare a son... another seed."
[L4] Genesis 16:15 names Abram as the father of the seed of Genesis 16:10. Genesis 4:25 names Adam as the father of Eve's "another seed." So these rows name a woman's seed with its father standing in the record. They fit C1.

## B. Jeremiah 22:30

[L1] Jeremiah 22:24: "though Coniah... were the signet upon my right hand, yet would I pluck thee thence."
[L3] Haggai 2:23: "O Zerubbabel, my servant, the son of Shealtiel, saith the LORD, and will make thee as a signet: for I have chosen thee." Jeremiah 18:8: "If that nation, against whom I have pronounced, turn from their evil, I will repent of the evil that I thought to do unto them." Luke 3:27: "which was the son of Zorobabel, which was the son of Salathiel."
[L4] The signet plucked from Coniah in Jeremiah 22:24 is set on Coniah's grandson in Haggai 2:23, "for I have chosen thee." Jeremiah 18:8 states the LORD's own rule for a pronounced sentence. Luke 3:27, the list the defender routes through, carries the same two names. So Jeremiah 22:30 fits a sentence the LORD himself answered at Haggai 2:23. It does not set Luke's line against Matthew's.

## C. "Before they came together" (Matthew 1:18) against C4

[L1] Matthew 1:18: "before they came together, she was found with child."
[L3] Matthew 1:24: "and took unto him his wife." Deuteronomy 20:7: "hath betrothed a wife, and hath not taken her."
[L2] "Took unto him" is *paralambanō* (G3880), "to receive near, i.e. associate with oneself (in any familiar or intimate act or relation)."
[L4] Deuteronomy 20:7 shows the betrothed "wife" and the later taking as two steps. Matthew 1:24 narrates that taking with *paralambanō*. So the coming together of Matthew 1:18 is the taking of 1:24, and the finding comes before it. Matthew 1:25 "knew her not till" covers the span after the taking. Through the espousal she is "Mary thy wife" (Matthew 1:20) and "his neighbour's wife" by law (Deuteronomy 22:24). Genesis 4:1, "Adam knew Eve his wife; and she conceived," gives the means. So Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal, as C4 holds.

## D. Matthew 1:19-20: what the angel answered

[L1] Matthew 1:20: "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." Its margin reads "conceived: Gr. begotten."
[L2] *Phobeō* (G5399), to be alarmed, takes as its object *paralambanō* (G3880), to take near.
[L3] 2 Samuel 7:14: "I will be his father, and he shall be my son." 1 Chronicles 28:6: "Solomon thy son... for I have chosen him to be my son."
[L4] The fear the angel answers is fear "to take unto thee," with the object named. The "for" clause grounds the taking: the child is the seed God claims as his son. 1 Chronicles 28:6 puts "thy son" and "my son" in one verse. So Matthew 1:20 fits a covenant claim spoken to "Joseph, thou son of David."

## E. Luke 1:35-37

[L1] Luke 1:32: "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David."
[L2] *Dio kai* means "on which account also."
[L4] The *dio kai* of verse 35 connects back to verse 32, not forward to a divine paternity of flesh. The title and "the throne of his father David" are given in Luke 1:32, before Mary asks "How shall this be" in Luke 1:34.

[L1] Luke 1:36-37: "thy cousin Elisabeth, she hath also conceived a son in her old age... For with God nothing shall be impossible."
[L3] Luke 1:13: "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son."
[L4] The sign the angel gives beside "nothing shall be impossible" is a conception whose father, Zacharias, is named at Luke 1:13. So Luke 1:36-37 fits God's power working inside a marriage with a named husband.

## F. "Joseph and his mother" (Luke 2:33)

[L1] Luke 2:33: "Joseph and his mother marvelled." Luke 2:41: "his parents went to Jerusalem every year."
[L3] Luke 2:43: "Joseph and his mother knew not of it." Luke 2:48: "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing."
[L2] *Patēr* (G3962), father, stands in Mary's words at Luke 2:48.
[L4] The same narrator writes "Joseph and his mother" at 2:33 and 2:43, and "his parents" at 2:41, which falls between them. Then the mother says "thy father." So Luke 2:33 names Joseph and fits the parents and the father of the same chapter.

## G. Hebrews 4:15 and 10:5

[L1] Hebrews 4:15: "in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin."
[L3] Hebrews 2:14: "he also himself likewise took part of the same." Jeremiah 1:5: "Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee." Jeremiah 1:1: "Jeremiah the son of Hilkiah."
[L4] Hebrews 4:15 bounds sin. Hebrews 2:14 says "likewise" of flesh. Jeremiah 1:5 has God forming a body in the belly, and Jeremiah 1:1 names that prophet's father. So "a body hast thou prepared me" (Hebrews 10:5; margin "or, thou hast fitted me") fits God's forming of a body whose father is named.
